topic_summary: Analysis of the Renaissance humanist project to reconstruct Classical Latin from medieval Latin, examining whether this represented continuous evolution from a living drifted vernacular or discontinuous reoccupation of a textually-preserved kernel. The contest centers on competing readings of 'correct Latin' by medieval users (living practice) versus humanist reconstructors (textual authority).

key_entities: Classical Latin (textually preserved form, 1st century BCE - 2nd century CE)
Humanist reconstructors (Petrarch, Valla, Bruni, Poggio, Erasmus)
Textual corpus (manuscripts recovered via ad fontes)
Pronunciation systems (medieval vernacular-influenced vs reconstructed classical)
Ciceronian movement (radical return to single classical model)
key_tensions: Living practice vs textual authority (medieval drift vs humanist reconstruction)
Continuity vs rupture (development claim vs discontinuous replacement)
Vitality vs rigidity (Poliziano's evolution vs Cortesi's Ciceronian purity)
Private usage vs public performance (humanists wrote vernacular-influenced Latin privately, classical publicly)
key_mechanisms: Textual criticism (manuscript recovery, editing, orthographic standardization)
Pedagogical reform (curriculum expansion, then Ciceronian narrowing)
key_absences: Native speaker testimony (no living Classical Latin speakers to adjudicate correctness)
Phonological evidence (pronunciation reconstruction based on orthography and meter, not recordings)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The Latin language as authoritative medium for learned discourse, law, and liturgy
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Correctness grounded in either living practice (medieval) or textual fidelity to classical corpus (humanist)

readings.commitment: Correct Latin is the evolved form shaped by continuous use, pronunciation, and practical needs
readings.authority_grounding: living practice / institutional continuity / Vulgate authority
readings.expected_structural_delta: Low extractiveness (ε ≤0.15); language serves users; drift is legitimate evolution; beneficiary is the practicing community; no victim set (evolution is not extraction)

readings.commitment: Correct Latin is the classical form recoverable from 1st-century BCE texts via philological reconstruction
readings.authority_grounding: textual authority / ad fontes / manuscript evidence
readings.expected_structural_delta: Moderate extractiveness (ε 0.30-0.45); reconstruction imposes costs on medieval users (retraining, delegitimization); beneficiary is humanist elite; victim is medieval practitioner whose competence is now 'incorrect'

readings.commitment: Correct Latin is exclusively Ciceronian usage; post-Ciceronian and medieval forms are corruption
readings.expected_structural_delta: High extractiveness (ε 0.55-0.70); radical narrowing of acceptable usage; beneficiary is Ciceronian faction (Cortesi); victim is broader humanist community (Poliziano) and all medieval users; suppresses linguistic vitality

omegas.description: The absence of native Classical Latin speakers creates an adjudication vacuum: no external authority can definitively resolve whether humanist reconstruction recovered the 'true' classical form or constructed a new standard. This vacuum is what makes the kernel contest possible—both readings claim correctness, but neither can appeal to living practice to validate their claim.
omegas.source: Deferred axis native_speaker_absence + Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory)

omegas.description: The user's D1 break question—whether reconstructed Classical Latin was reachable from medieval drift or a separate kernel reoccupied—cannot be definitively answered from the evidence. The humanists claimed continuity ('development of medieval forms') while their methods created discontinuity (pronunciation reform, orthographic purging). The contest may be irresolvable: reachability depends on whether you privilege the humanists' self-understanding (continuous) or their observable practices (discontinuous).
omegas.source: User's kernel contest framing + deferred axis continuity_vs_rupture

omegas.description: Poliziano's opposition to Ciceronian rigidity ('vitality of writing could not be limited by norms too rigid in imitation') suggests a fourth reading not selected for generation: Latin as living evolving standard that incorporates classical models without servile imitation. This reading would have moderate ε (extraction via elite gatekeeping but not radical narrowing) and might represent a synthesis position. Deferred due to limited textual evidence of institutional uptake.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) + research context on Poliziano vs Cortesi

omegas.description: Medieval Latin's grounding in Vulgate authority (Jerome's 4th-century translation) creates a competing textual authority that humanists had to navigate. The Vulgate was itself a translation from Greek/Hebrew, not 'pure' classical Latin, yet it carried ecclesiastical authority. How did humanists reconcile their classical purism with the Church's authoritative Latin text? This tension is not addressed in the research context and may represent a suppressed axis.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) + extraction anchor 'Vulgate influence'

omegas.description: Erasmus's reconstructed classical pronunciation was based on orthography and meter, not phonological recordings. How accurate was it? If significantly inaccurate, then humanist 'classical' Latin may have been a new constructed standard rather than a recovery. This uncertainty affects whether the humanist reading represents reoccupation of a preserved kernel or construction of a new one.
omegas.source: Extraction anchor 'pronunciation systems' + absence of phonological evidence

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. The kernel/reading decomposition successfully captures the structural contest. Three readings selected represent the full spectrum from living practice (low ε) through textual reconstruction (moderate ε) to Ciceronian purity (high ε). Deferred axes are genuinely redundant or under-evidenced, not suppressed due to availability bias.
